title: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night
description: It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs. The markets lending money to
body: It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs. The markets lending money to governments appear to be changing more fundamentally too.Over summer, the message has been made clear: countries will have to pay more to borrow cash.The immediate reason is the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, which has pushed up inflation and, in turn, raised expectations of higher interest rates in the world's major economies.Markets had assumed tensions would subside, and so too would oil and gas prices, ahead of the US midterm elections in November.It was wishful thinking, based on the hope that US President Donald Trump would want the conflict in the Middle East resolved well before Americans go to the polls. But that has not happened, leaving markets pricing in higher energy prices, a chronic Gulf crisis, higher inflation for longer - and so higher interest rates.But that is only part of the story.The bigger picture is rising demand for borrowing across the world - and not just from governments. Big tech companies are turning to the same bond markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars for investments in AI data centres.Over $219bn (£162bn) of debt has already been issued this year by the US "hyperscalers" such as Google, Amazon and Meta, nearly a third of it in currencies other than the dollar, including sterling.The total issued last year was $93bn, while before that it averaged less than $40bn a year. Some expect the tech giants to raise $400-$500bn from the bond markets this year. These are staggering sums, raising competition in the market and pushing up the price for governments.Looking east, there is another major borrower: Japan.It has the highest debt burden, relative to its GDP, of the major economies and is the biggest single lender to the US government. Until recently its central bank's interest rate was zero, but that has crept up to help combat rising inflation. As a result, its government bond yields have been pushed to 30-year highs. The declining value of the yen complicates things, but the bottom line is that there is a change afoot in the global flow of money.The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt". But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor. Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike. Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans."More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night

title: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death
description: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn -
body: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, having suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield, and Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37, and Peter Horvath, 38, all of Holywell Heights, appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court.The four Slovakian nationals have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also appeared in the same court charged with perverting the course of justice.All five defendants were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday. Tuesday's hearing was told the baby's body was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse and was wrapped in a towel inside a blue bag.Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson said the defendants had been accused of perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene.Earlier, police said two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remained on bail.Speaking ahead of the court hearing, Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl."I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation."We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course."Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries. Listen to highlights from South Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North

schema.headline: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death

title: South African airline behind daring stadium stunt cancels next flyby
description: The South African airline behind a stunt which saw two planes flying in close formation low over a packed stadium, has cancelled a similar operation t
body: The South African airline behind a stunt which saw two planes flying in close formation low over a packed stadium, has cancelled a similar operation this weekend.Airlink confirmed it had withdrawn its application for the display set to take place before South Africa's rugby match with New Zealand in Johannesburg on Saturday, citing a poor weather forecast.The airline's flying feat divided opinion, with some labelling the startling manoeuvre reckless while others praised the precision and expertise.It comes as the the country's aviation regulator said that while it had approved the application for the flyby, it was now reviewing the operation following "discussions in the media".Footage of last weekend's air show before the start of the match in Cape Town was shared around the world.Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50ft (15m) above the top of the stadium".From some angles the jets appeared very close to the roof of the DHL Stadium as they roared over amid coloured flare smoke.The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said on Wednesday it would review the incident."Following various discussions in the media relating to the events of the past weekend, the SACAA initiated compliance verifications, engaged the operator, obtained the Flight Data Recording downloads as well as other additional requirements," it said in a statement.It also revealed a flight simulator to practice for the Saturday flight was used as part of the approvals process.

schema.headline: South African airline behind daring stadium stunt cancels next flyby

title: Early release scheme set to free 2,500 prisoners by end of year
description: About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of th
body: About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying"."I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded. The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:From 10 November, 650 offenders serving up to three years and two monthsFrom 8 December, 550 offenders serving up to four years and three monthsFrom 12 January 2027, 600 offenders serving up to five years and nine monthsFrom 9 February, 500 offenders serving up to seven years and six monthsFrom 9 March, 200 offenders serving up to nine yearsFrom 13 April, 200 offenders serving up to 10 yearsFrom 11 May, 250 offenders serving up to 12 yearsFrom 9 June, 250 offenders serving more than 12 years.The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.Under the new rules this group will instead leave jail at the halfway point.The ministerial order lists all of the 71 crimes that are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, and sexual and grooming offences.Prisoners on a special form of extended sentence and those on life terms are excluded from the scheme.On Tuesday, the government explained it was creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.An investment of £110m, which is set to come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the BBC being released did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.Norris also said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

schema.headline: Early release scheme set to free 2,500 prisoners by end of year

title: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two sailors, Saudi Arabia says
description: Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.The Saudi
body: Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.The Saudi national shipping company, Bahri, confirmed on Wednesday that its vessel Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz".Sidr was hit by projectiles north of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, according to maritime security firms. A South Korean-owned supertanker, Senegal Prosperity, was reportedly struck east of Musandam around the same time.Iran has not responded to the Saudi allegation. But it said earlier that two tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while using an unauthorised route through the strait.The news of the sailors' deaths came after the US military carried out a wave of air strikes on Iran and Iranian forces targeted US bases in neighbouring Arab states with missiles and drones in their biggest exchange of fire since July.On Wednesday Iran's health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 injured in the US attacks. Iran has accused the US of a "war crime" over a strike that killed four people including two children at a wedding party in the southern city of Sirik. The US military said it was looking into the reports.Shipping company Bahri's statement said the unspecified "security incident" affecting Sidr happened in the Strait of Hormuz at around 23:40 local time (19:40 GMT) on Monday."It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident," it added. "The company extends its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathies to their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time."Later, the Saudi foreign ministry expressed the kingdom's condemnation of "Iran's targeting of the Saudi tanker (Sidr) while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz".It also condemned the recent Iranian attacks on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, and stressed the "need to halt escalation and respect the security and safety of international navigation", as well as the security of global energy supplies, national sovereignty, and international law.The statements were issued a day after maritime risk management and intelligence firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers each loaded with two million barrels of Saudi crude oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other as they transited outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday.Sidr was struck by "unknown projectiles" at 19:52 GMT about 16 nautical miles (30km) north-east of Khasab, Oman, while Senegal Prosperity was struck by "three unknown projectiles" about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, according to Marisks.The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency also reported two incidents in the same locations.On Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said in a statement that two oil tankers sought "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz before "striking mines and exploding". The vessels were "currently on fire", it added.The US military has not commented, but it said the latest strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members".The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.Despite the Iranian attacks, US President Donald Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday - a record daily total since the start of the war.

schema.headline: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two sailors, Saudi Arabia says

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
description: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig
body: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport."We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil"."We will not tolerate it," she said.While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said they were working on how to tighten enforcement of existing sanctions, and added there was broad support for an EU visa entry ban on Russian ex-combatants as well as stricter visa limits on Russian tourists.Several EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, are pushing for more than €193bn (£165bn) in frozen Russian assets to be used to help Ukraine. The idea was first planned at the end of 2025, and rejected by Belgium where the money is held. However, Belgium's position is unchanged because it fears being held financially liable by the courts.The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole."We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.High-voltage power lines were damaged near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at Skarżysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent men, women and children in Ukraine".

schema.headline: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig

title: Tara Davis-Woodhall 'lucky to be alive' after car crash
description: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.The 27-year-old America
body: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.The 27-year-old American was on her way to training last week when she was involved in a "very scary" head-on collision, leaving her with a "severe" concussion. While not ruling herself out of this month's inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, the reigning world champion says she has been unable to train since the accident."Luckily I walked away without any major injuries," Davis-Woodhall wrote on social media."At this point I'm working with my team and doctors to get healthy, but I'm not sure if I will be ready to compete at Ultimate Championships next week. More updates to come."Davis-Woodhall said her injuries were not life-threatening but that both cars, which were going at about 20mph, were written off.  "It's really unfortunate timing; I am at the peak of my training right now," she said. "I'm as fast as I've ever been. I'm as strong as I've ever been. So this decision is very difficult for me. I don't know where I am right now."The championships in Hungary start on 11 September, where athletes will compete for a top prize of £111,000.The competition brings together Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, as well as the year's leading performers in a three-day end-of-season event. Davis-Woodhall won long jump gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, before winning the Worlds in Tokyo a year later.

schema.headline: Tara Davis-Woodhall 'lucky to be alive' after car crash

title: More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says
description: ByEmma Pengelly and Richard Irvine-BrownBBC VerifyMore than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, ac
body: ByEmma Pengelly and Richard Irvine-BrownBBC VerifyMore than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.It brings the total number of Palestinians killed in the Strip since the 10 October ceasefire was declared to more than 1,300, including 301 children, the ministry says.Hamas and Israel agreed to halt the war after accepting US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. That plan included a suspension of "all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment".Since then, BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos which show the impact of Israeli strikes on locations including a beachside cafe, tents where displaced people have been sheltering, and a reported funeral procession in central Gaza.Recent months have been some of the most deadly according to the figures, with more than 100 people recorded killed each month between April and August.The health ministry attributes the deaths directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.The UN considers the figures reliable, and experts have told BBC Verify that their independent analysis is consistent with the ministry's data.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry's figures. It told BBC Verify there is "no basis to assume" that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity.It said it operates in "a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement", and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm "to the greatest extent possible".At the start of this year Israeli media reported that an Israeli security official acknowledged more than 70,000 people had been killed in the Gaza war, which it said included more than 20,000 combatants.'Ceasefire in name only'From the start of the ceasefire agreement on 10 October to the end of that month, the ministry recorded 251 deaths. Since then the deadly Israeli attacks have continued every month. The highest monthly death toll this year was recorded in July, when 152 people were killed including 21 children, according to the figures.The IDF says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident". It also says it has killed hundreds of military operatives since October.Conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled), which uses official statements, media reports and social media to verify attacks, says it has recorded around 200 Israeli strikes during the ceasefire that have reportedly killed Hamas operatives or other armed "militants" in targeted strikes.Acled said this includes commanders involved in planning the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war and killed around 1,200 people with 251 taken hostage.Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said "Gaza has seen a ceasefire in name only" since last October. He said the Israeli military has continued its almost daily air and drone strikes, and "though it claims to be targeting Hamas or imminent threats, it is Gaza's civilians that have continued to bear the brunt".This could now be a "central stumbling block" in international efforts to implement Trump's ceasefire deal, he added.The IDF told BBC Verify it "remains committed" to the ceasefire agreement and that there have been "continued violations and threats posed by Hamas and other terror organizations" in Gaza.Summer of deadly incidentsWarning: The following segment of this story contains graphic content which some readers might find distressing.Figure caption, Multiple deadly Israeli strikes in Gaza in  under 24 hoursBBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos of attacks in Gaza carried out since the ceasefire.In one, emergency services are seen attending to people in the aftermath of a strike at a beachside cafe in Gaza City on 18 August, where six people were killed, according to the health ministry. The next day nine people, including a 13-year-old, were reportedly killed in a strike on a police headquarters in the al-Tuffah neighbourhood.The IDF said it was targeting Hamas commanders and terrorists in the two incidents and that "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".One of the deadliest single incidents in July was a strike on a reported funeral procession in Nuseirat. Seven people were killed and 22 injured, according to the Al-Awda Hospital where casualties were taken. Several verified images show nine people covered in blood lying on the street. Two people appear to still be alive and are being treated by bystanders.The IDF said it was targeting a "significant military operative" of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group who was involved in the 7 October 2023 attacks.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Men assess scene of Israeli strike on high-rise block in Gaza City on 2 AugustIn a strike on an apartment block on the western edge of Gaza City overnight on 1 August, a pregnant woman, her husband and their young son were killed, according to local reports. Verified footage showed the body of an unborn baby in the rubble.A man searching the ruins said he had heard a strike overnight and saw smoke coming from the building. "I broke the door and went up and I found dead bodies scattered," he said. The IDF said it had targeted an acting Hamas commander.Child deaths 'absurd and devastating'UN agency Unicef has also reported more than 300 children have been killed since the ceasefire. The aid organisation has been tracking all available reports of incidents affecting children in Gaza, including via UN personnel on the ground.James Elder, Unicef global spokesperson, said the number of child deaths was "absurd and devastating".He added that hundreds more have been injured. "A ceasefire that paints such a grim picture can only be failing children."Unicef and other humanitarian organisations operating inside Gaza have also reported Israeli strikes on their workers since the ceasefire. This includes two water truck drivers contracted by Unicef killed in April by Israeli fire at the Mansoura water filling point in northern Gaza.The IDF said its soldiers "identified suspects approaching" the Yellow Line area during the incident, who were later identified as UN contractors who had not "coordinated in advance". Unicef said the drivers were carrying out routine water trucking operations with "no changes in movement or procedures".Aid Worker Security Database, whose figures have been cited by the UN and UK government, told BBC Verify it has recorded 22 aid workers killed in Gaza since 10 October 2025.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Palestinians grieve over bodies of people killed in an Israeli attack targeting a beachfront cafe in Gaza CityIndependent research group Airwars works to identify civilian deaths from a range of open sources including news agencies, NGOs and social media, matching names it finds to those published by the health ministry.Director Emily Tripp told BBC Verify the ministry's data on death tolls is consistent with its own tracking and research, and that it recorded more than 60 deadly incidents in July."This is the highest number of fatal incidents we've seen in a month since the ceasefire," Tripp said. "Our own findings point to an increasing number of civilian harm incidents a month."Professor Michael Spagat from Royal Holloway, University of London, is the chair of Every Casualty Counts, a charity that studies death tolls in wars. He told BBC Verify that the figures recorded by the health ministry are "testable" because it publishes names, ages and ID numbers of the dead.He said that since April, the monthly death toll in Gaza has been roughly double what was seen in December. "July was the worst month but even August's lower toll is still high compared with the November to March period," he added.Additional reporting Paul Brown, Benedict Garman and Lamees Altalebi

schema.headline: More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says

title: King Charles, Macron and Burnham arrive to view Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum
description: There was also some cross-Channel teasing about the outcome of the Norman invasion story, if not accusations of a stitch up.President Macron commented
body: There was also some cross-Channel teasing about the outcome of the Norman invasion story, if not accusations of a stitch up.President Macron commented at the finish of the tapestry on the "happy end, we're here", while Andy Burnham said: "Made in England, they couldn't bear to show the end… too difficult."The King, speaking inside the Great Court of the British Museum, said the opponents depicted in the tapestry - Normans and Anglo-Saxons - would have been delighted to see this togetherness between France and the UK - "two great nations, which share such fundamental values"."The tapestry's story is one of ambition and uncertainty, of oaths and journeys, of ships, councils, kings, comets and consequences," said the King."Yet it is not merely an English story, nor only a Norman one. Indeed, from the moment of its creation, it may have brought together our two peoples," he said, weaving in the historic importance of the artwork.Burnham joked about his own new role as prime minister - saying the tapestry "showed a new leader emerging from a northern territory and travelling to the south of England".Describing the tapestry as a "masterpiece", President Macron said a loan had first been proposed in the 1930s, but he was delighted that the idea had come to fruition.He spoke of the exhibition in London as an example of how "we are united" and a "reminder of what our countries can do if they join forces", addressing an audience including historian Dame Mary Beard and former prime minister Theresa May.The 70m (230ft) tapestry, originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.The King and Queen, Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel were given the chance to see the historic embroidery in the atmospheric darkness of the British Museum.It's displayed in a long glass illuminated cabinet, with the figures remarkably vivid for something almost a 1,000 years old, and visitors file along, following the story of the Norman invasion.The royal visitors had a close look at key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.It's filled with details of medieval life and the King commented on Normans pulling a cart with "an enormous amount of wine".Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the final scene, showing King Harold with an arrow in his eye, was what she found the most dramatic."We've just been talking to all the schoolchildren, and that's the bit that they really liked and really registered with them," she said."And it's amazing actually that a tapestry that is 1,000 years old can still inspire people to feel such emotion and capture such drama after all this time."Nandy said she was inspired by the way this epic depiction of conflict had "come to symbolise probably the biggest act of friendship on behalf of the French nation".Sending the tapestry to the British Museum was announced by Macron during a state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.There had been fears that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said display conditions at the British Museum were "ideal".The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres.It also allows viewers to get a clearer view of all the animals, plants and often bawdy images sewn around the margins of the main narrative.It is believed the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.The Bayeux Tapestry records a much earlier chapter in Anglo-French relations, when King William of Normandy fought King Harold for the throne of England.Using dyed wool stitched onto linen, it shows the competing claims to the throne, the Normans sailing across the Channel and the decisive Battle of Hastings, in which Harold was killed, allowing William the Conqueror to become monarch.The tapestry, believed to have been embroidered by English women for the new Norman rulers in the 1070s, includes 58 separate scenes, with 627 human figures, 737 animals, 37 ships and 23 trees, with a Latin narration accompanying the images.As part of this cultural diplomatic exchange, the UK is lending France one of the British Museum's prize exhibits - treasures from the Anglo-Saxon Sutton Hoo burial.There was strong demand for tickets to see the tapestry, with the exhibition already sold out until the end of 2026.The next tickets, covering visits between January and March 2027, will be available from the British Museum from 21 October.

schema.headline: King Charles, Macron and Burnham arrive to view Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum

title: Man City transfer news: New midfield but major Haaland gamble
description: Manchester City have completed their squad overhaul - including a fully revamped midfield - to the tune of £458m, a new Premier League record for a su
body: Manchester City have completed their squad overhaul - including a fully revamped midfield - to the tune of £458m, a new Premier League record for a summer window.But that eyewatering sum does not tell the full story.New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca received the full backing of director of football Hugo Viana in his first transfer window in charge after replacing Pep Guardiola. Indeed, City's record transfer fee was twice broken this summer.A joint-British record £125m was spent on Maresca's former Chelsea skipper Enzo Fernandez after £116m was committed on Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest. Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, was also brought in for £86m. The trio accounted for the bulk of City's summer incomings.The departures of captain Bernardo Silva, 2024 Ballon d'Or winner Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez means the City midfield has been completely transformed.Senior club sources are said to be delighted by the business done not only during the past couple of months but in January too, when plans were brought forward to sign long-term targets Antoine Semenyo and Marc Guehi.And if the clock is rewound further back, Manchester City's rebuild of the team that won the 2023 Champions League really began in January 2025 after a difficult start to that season.Just four players remain from the starting eleven and substitutes from the night they beat Inter Milan in Istanbul to win the continent's biggest club prize.Maresca now has the luxury of calling upon two established players in almost every position. City feel the squad is stronger at this point than at the beginning of last season which they believe has been achieved by remaining calm and trusting the transfer strategy.However some big questions remain. How will their new midfield signings all fit together?And, despite the vast amount of money spent, have they actually left themselves without a back-up to Erling Haaland?City's expenditure of £542m on new signings since the turn of the year will grab the headlines, but it often goes under the radar how well they do at selling fringe players.During this same period, they have recouped £334m, including a £75m for Savinho, who scored only two Premier League goals during his time at City, as well as £65m for Rodri and £52m for Reijnders.It gives City a net spend of £208m in 2026, which will be further bolstered by Tottenham's obligation to buy Omar Marmoush for £60m at the end of his loan spell next season.Sources had said during the summer that they were operating on a one-out, one-in policy and Maresca managed to replace almost every player that departed, aside from Nico Gonzalez and Marmoush.With the side well stocked at left-back, it is felt that Nico O'Reilly will play more in his natural midfield position to ease the Gonzalez gap.The club believe the record fee for Fernandez is justified by acquiring a proven winner at the highest level that will strengthen the midfield. Anderson was the summer's number one target, while 18-year-old Bouaddi is seen as having all the attributes to develop into a world class talent.City have won back-to-back games at the start of the Premier League season and Maresca will now have a selection dilemma each game as he possesses an embarrassment of riches to choose from.The question is how the Italian will now fit them all together.Image gallery 2Skip image galleryImage caption, When Bouaddi came on, he took up a holding midfield position, particularly in deep build-up play. Kovacic was positioned ahead of him as the right central midfielder.Slide 1 of 2, A screen grab from Manchester City against Crystal Palace illustrating their midfield shape focusing on the positions of Mateo Kovacic and Ayyoub Bouaddi.  , When Bouaddi came on, he took up a holding midfield position, particularly in deep build-up play. Kovacic was positioned ahead of him as the right central midfielder.Despite the positives around the recent window, Haaland is now City's only first-team striker.The 26-year-old is pivotal to the team, ending last season as the Premier League top scorer with 27 goals, and starting the new campaign by netting twice in as many games.But should Haaland be unavailable, what are City's options?Marmoush wanted to play regular first-team football and was allowed to join Tottenham, while 21-year-old Divin Mubama, who did well in pre-season, joined Championship side Southampton on loan.City believe they have enough flexibility from within their options to have not directly replaced Marmoush.Semenyo operates mainly from the right flank but is seen as an option at number nine, having played in the position during some cup games last season.Deadline day signing Ndiaye is another who can operate there and the £60m forward adds greater versatility and squad depth as someone who is a proven Premier League player.However, of the forward, attacking midfield and wide options, Semenyo is the only one to get into double figures in the Premier League in the last couple of seasons.Cherki, Jeremy Doku and Ndiaye have never hit that mark, while Foden is clearly capable, having hit 19 Premier League goals in 2023-24, but has struggled for consistent form in the last two seasonsUnless a couple of those step up, it could be one to watch if Haaland either needs to be rested or gets injured.

title: Nottingham attacks families not told 'stalker' had violent past
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were all killed by Valdo Calocane in a spate of attacks in No
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were all killed by Valdo Calocane in a spate of attacks in Nottingham on 13 June 2023ByDan Hunt and Asha PatelEast MidlandsUpdated 9 hours agoFamilies of the Nottingham attacks victims said police did not tell them a man who had taken an interest in them had a history of violence when he attempted to visit them.Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023. He tried to kill three others.Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, said he was told in 2025 that a man had visited his GP surgery in London. Emma Webber, Barnaby's mother, said he had also travelled to Somerset, but neither were informed of the man's history of mental ill health.Nottinghamshire Police said it had received a complaint and referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).The IOPC confirmed it had received a referral of a complaint from Nottinghamshire Police in relation to information the force allegedly withheld from the families of Calocane's victims about a potential witness who had tried to contact them.'Be transparent'Kumar told the BBC he was informed by Nottinghamshire Police in 2025 that a man from Nottingham, who had taken an interest in his family and the Webber family, had visited his surgery in London.He said police gave little to no details about the man, with no mention of his past mental health history."They [the police officers] said it was a very lowbrow thing. There was no assessment of risk to me or my family," he added."They didn't mention the word 'risk'."Kumar said it was only recently, as a result of ongoing investigations into Nottinghamshire Police, in relation to the attacks, that he was informed of further details about the man by the IOPC."Later, we found out from the IOPC that this guy was on the Prevent register, that he had been sectioned a few times or that he was known to be a violent offender," Kumar said."I'm angry. Don't place my wife, don't place my other child at risk. Do these people not realise the tragedy we've been through?"Just be transparent. That's all we wanted."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Grace's parents, Dr Sanjoy Kumar and Dr Sinead O'Malley-Kumar, have raised concerns about "minimal" information from policeSpeaking to BBC Radio 4, Grace's mother, Dr Sinead O'Malley-Kumar, said she was "absolutely flabbergasted" that police were aware of the man's behaviour in December 2024, but did not inform families until about a year later."And what's more concerning is that, as victims, we weren't given the proper information," she added."We do not know what this man looks like. Should he ring on our doorbell? Should he come to our place of work again? "The information has been minimal."The Times reports, external Barnaby Webber's parents were not told for 18 months that a stalker had travelled to Somerset to try to find them.Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, said in a social media post she was "furious"."Now we learn that another mentally ill man with a fixation on us and the  Nottingham case travelled to Somerset, including our home town, seeking out victims' families; and the police chose not to tell us," she said.'Should have been updated'A spokesperson for the IOPC said it was "assessing the referral" from Nottinghamshire Police to decide what further action was required."After originally receiving information from Nottinghamshire Police we spoke to a potential witness in January 2025 in connection with our investigation concerning the force's interactions with Calocane prior to the attacks," the spokesperson added."It was unclear whether Calocane was the suspect for the matters that had been reported to police by the witness and the information was assessed as not relevant to our inquiries."We did, however, make the force aware of the information provided by the witness so it could take the appropriate safeguarding measures."We recognised that the families should have been updated that we'd spoken to this witness at the time and acknowledged that in a recent update to them.A Nottinghamshire Police spokesperson said: "We received a complaint and due to the nature of the complaint referred the matter to the IOPC on August 24 and are awaiting their response. "Unfortunately, we cannot comment any further at this stage while an investigation is underway. We have updated the complainant throughout the process."Image source, Nottinghamshire PoliceImage caption, Calocane, now 34, is currently serving an indefinite hospital orderCalocane pleaded guilty to three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder in November 2023.He was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024. A public statutory inquiry, which is examining the lead-up to the attacks and decisions taken in the aftermath is set to resume in September.What later emerged was a series of failings by authorities, including the police and mental health services - which Calocane was known to - prompting calls for a statutory public inquiry.The Nottingham Inquiry heard from more than 100 witnesses as the lead-up to the attacks, the investigation that followed and the aftermath were examined.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Nottingham

title: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Nigel Farage tells BBC
description: Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's finances.Speaking to the BBC a
body: Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's finances.Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and £5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.Farage acknowledged his party's poll ratings had taken a hit compared to last year, but said it would rebound and still had "every chance" of winning the next general election.Reform's annual conference begins in Birmingham on Thursday, with both Farage and the party facing renewed questions over money.A parliamentary investigation into £5m he received from major Reform donor Christopher Harborne was relaunched following Farage's re-election in Clacton, after a by-election he called in the Essex seat.The Metropolitan Police is also investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.The police probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell.It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.Asked if he knew whether or not money donated by Fiona Cottrell had come from her son George, Farage said he was not "involved in the transactions".However, he added that he "had been told it's her money". Reform has insisted it has always complied with donations rules.He added: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society. If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do"."There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat."There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing."So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour. "People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything." Farage said he expected it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed by Parliament's standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg as part of his probe into whether he should have publicly declared the £5m he received from Harborne.He continued to insist the sum, which he says was a personal gift, did not require registration under Commons rules.He added he had "no questions" about Greenberg's impartiality, but hit out at the "political composition" of the standards committee that will recommend what action should be taken on his findings.The 14-member panel includes seven MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats, but none from Reform UK.He added: "Have you seen who's on the committee? I think we know the outcome already. I'm not going to say anything more than that.""To be judged by members of Parliament by other political parties who you're fighting against in by-elections or general elections, I think that raises a question, I really do," he added. Elsewhere in his interview, Farage acknowledged that Reform was "down a bit" in its poll ratings compared to 2025, after failing to win in by-elections this year including Gorton and Denton and Makerfield, which saw Andy Burnham's re-election as an MP ahead of becoming Labour leader. But he added that "markets don't move in straight lines", adding that the party still had "every chance" of winning the next general election, due by 2029.He said the party was continuing to look "outside of the political sphere" to fill frontbench positions, following a raft of appointments earlier this year to senior posts within the party.And he said he continued to hold to his previous prediction there would be an election next spring "forced on the government" by the markets, amid rising costs to public borrowing.Reform's conference, he said, would be a chance for the party to set out details of the "fundamental changes" it would make within 100 days of winning power.He added that whilst his and other parties had announced a number of new policies in recent weeks, what most interested voters was who is "actually going to deliver" than the specifics of individual policies.

schema.headline: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Nigel Farage tells BBC

title: DNB: Netherlands bank moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move
description: The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "incre
body: The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest".DNB said on Wednesday that 86 tonnes of gold had been removed from the US and Canada in a complex operation that took several months. It is now being held by the Bank of England, where the precious metal can be traded more easily "in a crisis situation".Bank president Olaf Sleijpen said the move was "necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness".The decision comes amid an ongoing trade dispute between the US and Canada, with both countries announcing fresh tariffs on each other after failed trade talks.DNB said the transfer, which took place between March and August, saw 27 tonnes of gold bars moved from New York and Ottawa to Zeist in the Netherlands. A similar quantity and quality was then moved to London, with no need to melt the bars down.Exactly how so much gold was transported across the Atlantic Ocean has not been revealed.The rest of the transfer was carried out by selling the gold in New York, and repurchasing it in London, the bank said, external."Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation," the statement said.DNB did not confirm what it was referring to with its mention of "geopolitical unrest" but the US economy remains in an uncertain position due to the country's ongoing war with Iran, which has impacted global trade.Canada, meanwhile, has been hit hard by US tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles as well as an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods announced in August. DNB said that gold that is held with the Bank of England "is regarded as the world's most easily tradable gold," and therefore more readily available in a crisis than if it was still in the US or Canada.Prior to Wednesday's announcement, the DNB held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa. This has now fallen to 18.5% in both countries.The total Dutch gold stock was 612.4 tonnes at the end of 2025 and has been valued at €72.2 billion, DNB said.The bank's share of gold in London has increased from 18.1% to 32.1% after the move, while it still holds 30.8% of its reserves in the Netherlands.

schema.headline: DNB: Netherlands bank moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move

title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
description: Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of
body: Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.He blamed the previous Tory government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, meaning Wednesday was the first time he had faced Badenoch at PMQs.Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998. This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain its spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK,  announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill."The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said."He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts."Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality."I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government.Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict."Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said."Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years."How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages."She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."In the Tory reshuffle, Andrew Griffith replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor.Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."

schema.headline: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
